questions.question: What is the oldest printed book of Japan, printed in AD 868 containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations?
questions.explanation: The Buddhist Diamond Sutra, printed in Japan in AD 868, is universally recognized as the oldest surviving dated printed book in the world. Discovered inside the Dunhuang caves, this remarkable artifact consists of six woodblock-printed sheets of mulberry paper containing Buddhist sutra Sanskrit-Chinese calligraphy text alongside an intricate woodcut frontispiece illustration depicting the Buddha preaching to his elderly disciple Subhuti. It reflects the ancient East Asian mastery of block printing centuries before Europe.

questions.question: In 1295, which great Italian explorer returned to Italy after years of exploration in China and brought back the knowledge of woodblock printing?
questions.explanation: In 1295, the Venetian merchant explorer Marco Polo returned to Venice after spending over seventeen years exploring China, the Silk Route, and the imperial Mongol court of Kublai Khan. Among the sophisticated Eastern technologies he introduced to Italy was the Chinese art of woodblock printing. Italian craftsmen and book publishers embraced this technique, mass-producing printed playing cards, religious prints, and inexpensive paper books, which rapidly diffused across trade routes into Germany, France, and the Netherlands.

questions.question: What was the first book printed by Johann Gutenberg on his newly invented movable metal type printing press in Mainz around 1448?
questions.explanation: Johann Gutenberg developed the first mechanized movable type printing press in Mainz, Germany, around 1448, adapting the screw-lever mechanics of olive and wine presses. The first comprehensive literary masterpiece printed on Gutenberg's press was the Latin 42-line Bible (known as the Gutenberg Bible) completed around 1455. Gutenberg printed approximately 180 copies across three years on handmade paper and vellum—a production velocity that was astonishingly fast compared to traditional monastic manuscript scribes.

questions.question: In 1517, the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote 'Ninety-Five Theses' criticizing many of the practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church, posting it on the church door at:
questions.explanation: In 1517, the German Augustinian monk and theology professor Martin Luther wrote his fiery 'Ninety-Five Theses' (Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences) condemning corrupt Roman Catholic Church practices, particularly the commercial sale of papal indulgences for remission of sins. Luther posted a printed copy on the heavy oak doors of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, challenging scholars to a public theological debate. Printed vernacular copies were rapidly reproduced and circulated across Germany, igniting the Reformation.

questions.question: Who declared that 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one'?
questions.explanation: Deeply awed by the revolutionary speed with which his German translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in a fortnight, Protestant reformer Martin Luther famously declared: 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.' Luther recognized that Gutenberg's mechanized movable press was an unstoppable democratic equalizer that broke the Catholic Church's Latin monopoly on biblical scriptures, enabling ordinary literate citizens to read, interpret, and practice religious faith independently without papal priests.

questions.question: Who was Menocchio, hauled before the Roman Catholic Inquisition in the sixteenth century and executed for heresy?
options: A German monk who translated the New Testament
A French royal censor who banned Voltaire's writings
A Dutch cartographer who drew maps of the Americas
An Italian miller who reinterpreted the Bible and developed radical views on God and Creation
questions.explanation: Menocchio (Domenico Scandella) was a literate village miller from northern Italy who devoured vernacular books, folk tales, and popular translations of the Bible made available by the 16th-century print revolution. Comparing printed texts with his daily rustic experiences, Menocchio formulated a radical, heretical cosmology: he declared that God and the universe emerged from primordial chaos just as maggots and cheese emerge from curdled milk. Alarmed by his subversive views, the Roman Catholic Inquisition arrested, tortured, and executed him.

questions.question: Alarmed by heretical literature and independent interpretations of faith, the Roman Catholic Church began maintaining the official 'Index of Prohibited Books' from:
questions.explanation: The explosion of vernacular printed literature, Protestant theology, and popular anti-clerical tracts deeply alarmed the Roman Catholic Church hierarchy. Fearing that uncontrolled print gave uneducated commoners and heretics the dangerous power to question religious dogma, church authorities instituted strict pre-publication censorship controls over European printers and booksellers. In 1558 (under Pope Paul IV), the Roman Catholic Church officially published the first authoritative 'Index of Prohibited Books' (Index Librorum Prohibitorum).

questions.question: In England, small, cheap pocket-sized booklets sold by travelling pedlars for a single penny were known as:
questions.explanation: In eighteenth-century England, the dramatic rise in working-class literacy fueled an insatiable popular appetite for cheap, accessible reading materials. Publishers responded by producing 'chapbooks'—pocket-sized booklets printed on coarse paper and priced at just one penny (a penny chapbook) so that even impoverished urban artisans and farmhands could afford them. These booklets were carried across remote countryside villages by itinerant pedlars known as 'chapmen', featuring folklore, murder ballads, historical tales, and almanacs.

questions.question: In France, cheap, low-priced popular books bound in low-cost blue paper covers were called:
questions.explanation: In eighteenth-century France, publishers established a wildly successful mass-market publishing genre known as the 'Bibliothèque Bleue' (the Blue Library). These were compact, low-priced pocketbooks printed on inexpensive, coarse grayish paper and bound in flimsy, distinctive blue sugar-paper covers. Distributed across rural provinces by travelling colporteurs (pedlars), they catered to newly literate peasants and urban wage-earners, containing abridged chivalric romances, moral allegories, folk tales, and practical advice.

questions.subtopic: Mercier on the Power of Print
questions.question: Which French eighteenth-century novelist proclaimed: 'Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!'?
questions.explanation: Louis-Sébastien Mercier, an influential 18th-century French Enlightenment novelist and dramatist, celebrated the printing press as the most unstoppable engine of intellectual liberty and historical progress. Convinced that mass literacy and the diffusion of Enlightenment philosophy would inevitably destroy monarchical tyranny and clerical superstition, Mercier passionately proclaimed in his writings: 'Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!'—a prophetic anticipation of the French Revolution of 1789.

questions.question: By the mid-nineteenth century, who perfected the power-driven cylindrical press capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour, specially used for newspapers?
options: Richard M. Hoe of New York
questions.explanation: By the mid-nineteenth century, the insatiable global demand for daily newspapers and commercial periodicals demanded mechanical breakthroughs. Richard March Hoe of New York perfected the rotary cylindrical printing press in the 1840s. By mounting movable curved type onto a massive revolving central cylinder that pressed against smaller impression rollers, Hoe's power-driven rotary press printed up to 8,000 newspaper sheets per hour, shattering old flat-bed limits and ushering in modern mass-circulation daily journalism.

questions.question: The printing press first came to India in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century with:
questions.explanation: The printing press made its historical debut in the Indian subcontinent in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century, brought by Portuguese Jesuit missionaries. Jesuit priests mastered indigenous Indian languages to preach Christian doctrine to coastal populations: they printed the first Konkani and Marathi religious catechisms and grammars by 1556–1579. By 1674, approximately fifty theological books had been printed in Konkani and Kanara, marking the formal arrival of European typography on Indian soil.

questions.question: In 1780, who began editing the 'Bengal Gazette', a private weekly English magazine described as 'a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none'?
questions.explanation: In January 1780, an eccentric Irish-born printer named James Augustus Hicky founded the 'Bengal Gazette' (also known as the Calcutta General Advertiser) in Calcutta, representing the first printed English weekly newspaper in India. Proudly declaring his journal 'a weekly political and commercial paper open to all parties, but influenced by none', Hicky published biting satirical critiques, private gossip, and exposes of colonial corruption targeting Governor-General Warren Hastings, leading to Hicky's eventual arrest and press seizure.

questions.question: Which influential weekly newspaper did Raja Rammohun Roy publish from 1821 to debate social and religious reforms?
questions.explanation: Raja Rammohun Roy, the pioneering reformist often hailed as the father of modern Indian renaissance, founded the historic weekly Bengali newspaper 'Sambad Kaumudi' in 1821. Roy utilized print as a powerful weapon of rational social reform, publishing scholarly arguments dismantling cruel orthodox Hindu customs—particularly the brutal practice of Sati (widow-burning), female infanticide, child marriage, and hereditary caste untouchability. In response, Hindu conservatives launched the rival weekly 'Samachar Chandrika' in 1822.

questions.question: Founded in 1867, which Islamic seminary in North India published thousands of fatwas guiding Muslim conduct in daily life and explaining Islamic doctrines?
questions.explanation: Founded in 1867 in the Saharanpur district of Uttar Pradesh amidst post-1857 colonial anxieties, the Deoband Seminary (Darul Uloom Deoband) mobilized modern print technology to preserve orthodox Islamic theological traditions. questions.question: Who wrote 'Amar Jiban' (1876), the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language, having learned to read secretly in her kitchen?
questions.explanation: Rashsundari Debi, an orthodox Vaishnava housewife in rural East Bengal (now Bangladesh), shattered rigorous patriarchal taboos by secretly teaching herself to read and write in her smoky kitchen by the flickering light of cooking fires, stealing glimpses of manuscripts while cooking. In 1876, she published 'Amar Jiban' ('My Life'), which holds the historic distinction of being the first full-length autobiography ever published in the Bengali language, offering a moving account of women's domestic subjugation.

questions.question: In 1882 in Maharashtra, who published 'Stripurushtulna' ('A Comparison Between Women and Men') criticizing the social inequalities and double standards imposed on women?

questions.question: In 1871, Jyotirao Phule wrote 'Gulamgiri' ('Slavery') exposing caste oppression, dedicating his book to:
options: The Americans who fought to abolish black slavery in the American Civil War
The peasants of the Russian revolution
questions.explanation: In 1871, the visionary non-Brahman social revolutionary Jyotirao Govindrao Phule published his seminal Marathi treatise 'Gulamgiri' ('Slavery'). Phule exposed the historical origins of Brahmanical caste supremacy, arguing that the Aryan conquerors had subjugated the indigenous inhabitants and constructed the oppressive caste hierarchy to maintain perpetual dominance. Phule famously dedicated 'Gulamgiri' to the American abolitionists who had fought in the American Civil War to liberate enslaved Black Americans.

questions.question: The repressive Vernacular Press Act passed by the British colonial government in 1878 was modeled on the:
questions.explanation: In 1878, the colonial government under Viceroy Lord Lytton passed the repressive Vernacular Press Act to muzzle the burgeoning nationalist movement. Modelled directly on the authoritarian Irish Press Laws, the Act empowered British district magistrates to censor vernacular newspapers, demand financial security deposits, and confiscate printing presses, paper, and equipment if any journal published content deemed seditious or critical of British colonial governance, exempting English-language colonial papers.

questions.question: Which nationalist leader was imprisoned in 1908 for writing with deep sympathy in his Marathi newspaper 'Kesari' about deported Punjab revolutionaries, sparking nationwide strikes?
questions.explanation: Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, the staunch radical leader of the Indian National Congress, mobilized the vernacular press to ignite militant anti-colonial resistance. Editing the influential Marathi weekly newspaper 'Kesari', Tilak penned scathing, fearless editorials in 1908 sympathizing with Bengal revolutionaries and condemning British atrocities in the wake of the Muzaffarpur bombing. Tilak was arrested for sedition, convicted by a biased colonial court, and sentenced to six years of hard labor in Mandalay prison in Burma.
